Optional<Integer> composes with generic Optional operations and may fit better when the value is already part of an object-oriented generic pipeline. Neither should be used automatically for fields or serialized schemas; framework support and null representation matter. I choose based on boundary contract, generic composition and measured allocation needs rather than assuming the primitive form is always faster.

followups.q: Does OptionalInt have map like Optional<T>?
followups.a: Its API is specialized and does not provide the same generic map composition surface.

followups.q: Should a JSON DTO automatically use OptionalInt?
followups.a: No; serializer and wire-contract behavior must be considered explicitly.

questions.trap: Treating primitive Optional variants as universal replacements for nullable fields or generic Optional values.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; API surface and framework support depend on the specific use.

questions.question: What does Collectors.toUnmodifiableList guarantee compared with Stream.toList?
questions.answer: Collectors.toUnmodifiableList, added in Java 10, collects into an unmodifiable list and rejects null elements. Stream.toList, added in Java 16, also returns an unmodifiable list but has its own specified null behavior and result contract. Neither promises a mutable ArrayList, and unmodifiable structure does not make contained objects immutable. I choose the API available at the project's Java release and verify null policy when the input can contain nulls. If a mutable result is required, I collect explicitly to a mutable implementation instead of depending on a collector's unspecified concrete type.

followups.q: Does Collectors.toUnmodifiableList accept null elements?
followups.a: No, it rejects null elements.

followups.q: Does Stream.toList promise a mutable result?
followups.a: No, its result is unmodifiable.

questions.trap: Assuming these APIs are interchangeable without checking Java baseline, null handling and mutability.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; Java 10/16 API distinctions, Java 21 baseline.

questions.question: How should a resource-backed stream such as Files.lines be closed?
questions.answer: Some streams are backed by resources and must be closed, including Files.lines. I use try-with-resources around the stream so the underlying file resource is released whether processing completes normally or fails. A terminal operation does not universally close every stream source, so I do not rely on collection-style streams to share this lifecycle behavior. Short-circuiting may stop traversal early, making explicit closure even more important. I also consider I/O exceptions, charset and large-file processing. The stream abstraction does not remove ownership responsibility for the resource from which it was created.

followups.q: Does findFirst automatically close every stream?
followups.a: No. Resource-backed streams should be explicitly closed by their owner.

followups.q: Why use try-with-resources for a file stream?
followups.a: It releases the underlying resource on normal completion and exceptional exits.

questions.trap: Assuming any terminal stream operation closes files or other source resources automatically.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses stream lifecycle and supplied ETL context.

questions.question: What is Stream.onClose for, and when does its handler run?
questions.answer: onClose registers a close handler on a stream, typically to connect stream closure with cleanup for a resource-backed source. The handler runs when close is invoked, not merely because a terminal operation finishes. If several handlers are registered, they are invoked in registration order, and exceptions from handlers affect close behavior. The code that owns the stream should close it, commonly through try-with-resources. I do not use onClose for ordinary business side effects or assume it runs if the stream is abandoned without closure. Resource ownership should remain visible at the API boundary.

followups.q: Does onClose run automatically after count?
followups.a: No. The stream must be explicitly closed.

followups.q: Where should resource closure usually be expressed?
followups.a: At the owning scope, often with try-with-resources.

questions.trap: Attaching cleanup to onClose but never closing the stream that owns the handler.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; handler exception behavior should be checked for unusual cleanup chains.

questions.question: How do guarded patterns refine a type case in a Java 21 switch?
questions.answer: A guarded pattern adds a boolean condition to a type or record pattern case, allowing the switch to distinguish values of the same structural type by an additional rule. In Java 21 the guard uses when syntax. Cases should be ordered so more specific guarded cases are reachable before broader patterns that would subsume them. A guard can reference pattern variables, which makes validation and classification concise, but complex guards can hide policy and exceptions. I keep guards pure and extract substantial business rules into named methods. Exhaustiveness still needs a final strategy for all values in the matched domain.

followups.q: Can a guard use the pattern variable?
followups.a: Yes; the variable is available in its case guard and body.

followups.q: What can make a later pattern case unreachable?
followups.a: An earlier broader pattern may already match all values the later case could accept.

questions.trap: Writing overlapping switch patterns in an order that makes a specific case unreachable.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; Java 21 syntax should be compiled at the target source level.

questions.question: How should null be handled in modern switch expressions and pattern switches?
questions.answer: A switch over a reference value should have an explicit null policy. Traditional switch behavior may throw NullPointerException for a null selector, and type patterns do not match null. Modern pattern switches can include an explicit case null where supported by the target language level. I decide whether null is invalid, maps to a domain fallback or represents a separate state, then encode that choice visibly. A default case for non-null unmatched variants is not automatically a null handler. This distinction prevents an apparently exhaustive switch from silently assuming every value is non-null.

followups.q: Does default necessarily match null?
followups.a: No. Null handling is distinct and should be written explicitly where the switch form supports it.

followups.q: What should happen for invalid external enum input?
followups.a: Validate or map it at the boundary according to the API contract instead of relying on a switch default accidentally.

questions.trap: Assuming a default branch is a universal null case across Java switch forms.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; exact switch null behavior depends on switch form and Java release.

questions.question: What changed about the default charset in modern Java, and why should APIs still name it?
questions.answer: Starting with Java 18, UTF-8 became the standard default charset for Java APIs that use the default charset, improving consistency across platforms. Older runtimes and compatibility modes may behave differently, and code that relies on a default can still obscure an important file or protocol contract. I explicitly name the charset for persisted interchange data, signatures and external protocols so intent remains stable across runtime targets. This change does not normalize Unicode or guarantee that an external file actually uses UTF-8. I verify the deployed JDK and test malformed byte handling where data integrity matters.

followups.q: Does Java 18's default make explicit charset selection unnecessary?
followups.a: No; explicit encoding documents the contract and supports older or specially configured runtimes.

followups.q: Does UTF-8 default normalize text?
followups.a: No. Encoding and Unicode normalization are separate operations.

questions.trap: Assuming every runtime targeted by an application uses the Java 18 default behavior.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; default-charset behavior depends on runtime release and compatibility configuration.

questions.question: How should a team adopt Java 9-21 language features in a multi-module service?
questions.answer: I separate the JDK used to run the build from the source and target compatibility level, then verify how the build tool configures compilation and runtime tests. A feature can be available in the local JDK but unavailable to a deployed runtime or downstream module. I check library and framework support, CI images, container base images and production rollout before using newer syntax in shared APIs. Preview features require special compiler and runtime flags and should not be treated as permanent language contracts. A gradual upgrade needs repeatable CI validation across every module that consumes the changed classes.

followups.q: Does compiling locally with Java 21 prove production supports a feature?
followups.a: No. Production runtime and configured source/target levels must also support it.

followups.q: Can preview syntax be used without special flags?
followups.a: Preview features require the relevant compiler and runtime enablement and carry release-specific constraints.

questions.trap: Confusing the installed JDK version with the application's supported language and runtime baseline.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; applies to release engineering and should be checked against the repository's actual build configuration.

questions.question: How do Optional.of and Optional.ofNullable differ when given null?
questions.answer: Optional.of requires a non-null value and throws NullPointerException if passed null, making an unexpected null visible immediately. Optional.ofNullable accepts either a value or null and converts null to Optional.empty. I choose based on the source contract: use of when null violates an invariant, and ofNullable when nullable input is a normal representation of absence. Applying ofNullable everywhere can silently hide a programming defect, while using of on uncontrolled data can turn a recoverable absence into an exception. I keep this conversion at the boundary where the null policy is decided.

followups.q: What does Optional.ofNullable(null) return?
followups.a: Optional.empty.

followups.q: Why not always use ofNullable?
followups.a: It can hide a null that violates an invariant and should instead fail visibly.

questions.trap: Converting every unexpected null into empty and erasing the distinction between defect and legitimate absence.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Optional GAP.

questions.question: When should a stream use findFirst rather than findAny?
questions.answer: findFirst returns the first element in encounter order when the source has one, while findAny may return any element and is explicitly nondeterministic to allow more execution freedom, especially in parallel pipelines. Both are short-circuiting terminal operations and return Optional because the stream may be empty. If order has business meaning, I use findFirst and preserve that ordering through the pipeline. If any match is acceptable, findAny expresses that weaker requirement. I avoid depending on which value findAny returns in tests or production decisions, and remember that unordered sources have no meaningful first element contract.

followups.q: Does findAny promise the same element on every run?
followups.a: No. It may return any element, particularly with parallel execution.

followups.q: What if the stream is empty?
followups.a: Both methods return Optional.empty.

questions.trap: Using findAny when the business rule requires the earliest or otherwise ordered match.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Streams GAP.

questions.question: What do summarizingInt and averagingInt provide beyond a simple sum?
questions.answer: summarizingInt collects count, sum, minimum, maximum and average into an IntSummaryStatistics result in one traversal. averagingInt computes an average directly, while summingInt returns a numeric sum. These collectors make the desired aggregate explicit and avoid manually maintaining several mutable counters in stream callbacks. The sum uses int arithmetic and can overflow, while average is represented as a double and has floating-point precision limits. I choose long-based variants or domain-specific checked arithmetic when ranges demand it, and define behavior for an empty input, where average is not a meaningful numeric result.

followups.q: What does summarizingInt return?
followups.a: An IntSummaryStatistics value containing count, sum, minimum, maximum and average.

followups.q: Does summingInt detect integer overflow?
followups.a: No; the underlying int arithmetic can overflow.

questions.trap: Assuming a collector's numeric type automatically matches the domain's maximum possible value.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Streams GAP.

questions.question: What do CONCURRENT, UNORDERED and IDENTITY_FINISH mean for a Collector?
questions.answer: Collector characteristics describe properties that can let the stream implementation optimize collection. CONCURRENT indicates the accumulator can be called concurrently on the same result container under the collector's conditions; UNORDERED means the result does not depend on encounter order; IDENTITY_FINISH means the accumulation container can be used directly as the final result without a finisher conversion. These are semantic promises, not performance hints to set casually. A false characteristic can produce incorrect results. I use standard collectors by default and declare custom characteristics only after proving the accumulator, combiner and result contract satisfy them under parallel execution.

followups.q: Does CONCURRENT mean any shared mutable collector is safe?
followups.a: No. The characteristic is a contract that the collector's accumulator supports concurrent use under specified conditions.

followups.q: What does IDENTITY_FINISH allow?
followups.a: The accumulation container can be used as the result without applying a distinct finisher transformation.

questions.trap: Adding collector characteristics to encourage parallelism without implementing their required semantics.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; custom collector contracts require careful review and testing.

questions.question: How do Comparator.comparing and thenComparing improve Java 8 sorting code?
questions.answer: Comparator.comparing builds an ordering from a key-extraction function, and thenComparing adds tie-breakers when the primary keys compare equal. This makes multi-field ordering declarative and easier to review than nested comparison arithmetic. Primitive-specialized helpers such as comparingInt can avoid boxing in some cases. I make null ordering explicit, use stable business identifiers as tie-breakers when deterministic output matters, and ensure extracted keys remain stable during sorting. The composed comparator must still obey transitivity and consistency. I prefer this approach for ordinary object ordering, but keep a custom comparator when domain rules need a clear named implementation.

followups.q: Why add thenComparing?
followups.a: It establishes a secondary ordering when earlier comparison keys are equal.

followups.q: Does comparingInt always make sorting faster?
followups.a: Not necessarily; it avoids a boxing path in relevant cases, but workload performance should be measured.

questions.trap: Stopping after a non-unique primary key when deterministic ordering is required.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; Java 8 API, directly addresses supplied design-pattern and Streams preparation gaps.

questions.question: What ordering and lifecycle behavior should be considered with Stream.concat?
questions.answer: Stream.concat creates a lazily concatenated stream that emits elements from the first stream followed by elements from the second, preserving encounter order when both inputs have it. It does not deduplicate or merge matching elements. Closing the concatenated stream closes both input streams, so resource ownership should be clear when either input is resource-backed. The concatenated result should be consumed once and closed when needed. For many streams, repeatedly nesting concat can create an unwieldy pipeline; flattening a stream of streams may be clearer. I use concat for a small, explicit pair of compatible streams.

followups.q: Does concat remove duplicate elements?
followups.a: No. It appends the second stream's elements after the first without deduplication.

followups.q: What happens when the concatenated stream is closed?
followups.a: Its close action closes both input streams.

questions.trap: Assuming concat sorts, deduplicates or automatically closes the result after a terminal operation.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; resource-backed inputs require explicit closure of the resulting stream.

questions.question: When should Collectors.toMap use a map supplier in addition to a merge function?
questions.answer: The merge-function overload defines what happens when multiple elements produce the same key. The map-supplier overload additionally chooses the concrete result map, for example a TreeMap when sorted keys are required or a LinkedHashMap when encounter order is required. I provide both decisions explicitly when duplicate policy and result ordering matter, and ensure the supplier creates a fresh empty map for each collection. The merge function must reflect a deterministic business rule, not merely suppress an exception. If an unmodifiable result is required, I choose a finishing step or factory that establishes that contract after accumulation.

followups.q: Does the map supplier define duplicate resolution?
followups.a: No; the merge function defines how colliding values are combined.

followups.q: What must a map supplier return?
followups.a: A new empty map suitable for this collection operation.

questions.trap: Assuming the map supplier also resolves duplicate keys or ordering-independent value conflicts.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Streams GAP.

questions.question: When should a stream use mapToInt or mapToLong instead of map?
questions.answer: map transforms each element into another object-stream element, while mapToInt and mapToLong produce primitive streams with numeric terminals and avoid boxing each mapped value in the stream representation. I use them when the next operations are numeric, such as sum, average or range aggregation. If downstream code needs wrapper objects or generic composition, boxing back with boxed may be appropriate. Primitive specialization does not eliminate overflow or precision concerns, and performance depends on the whole pipeline. I make numeric width explicit so a convenient int stream does not silently exceed the domain's range.

followups.q: How do you convert an IntStream to Stream<Integer>?
followups.a: Use boxed(), accepting the conversion to wrapper values.

followups.q: Does mapToInt protect against sum overflow?
followups.a: No. IntStream.sum uses int arithmetic and can overflow.

questions.trap: Choosing int specialization for convenience when the numeric range requires long or arbitrary precision.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Streams GAP.

questions.question: What should be considered when choosing between Stream.of and Arrays.stream?
questions.answer: Stream.of accepts varargs values and creates an object stream of the supplied elements, while Arrays.stream is an explicit source adapter for an array and has overloads for primitive arrays that produce primitive streams. Passing an array to a varargs method can be interpreted as the varargs array itself, which is normally flattened into its elements but can be subtle for generic or single-array-element intent. I choose the API that makes the source shape clear and consider whether primitive specialization matters. Empty arrays, null arrays and arrays as elements should be tested where overload resolution could surprise callers.

followups.q: What does Arrays.stream(intArray) return?
followups.a: An IntStream over the primitive int values.

followups.q: How can an array be represented as one stream element?
followups.a: Use an explicit wrapper or type shape that prevents varargs from treating it as the argument array.

questions.trap: Assuming Stream.of and Arrays.stream have identical overload behavior for primitive arrays and array-valued elements.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; overload behavior should be confirmed with the exact declared array type.

questions.question: Why can a stream terminal operation not generally be repeated on the same stream?
questions.answer: A stream represents a one-shot traversal pipeline. A terminal operation consumes it, and a later attempt to run another terminal operation on the same stream is invalid and typically throws IllegalStateException. Some sources can create a fresh stream repeatedly, such as a collection's stream method, but other sources may be stateful or resource-backed and cannot be replayed safely. If two results are needed, I either derive them in one collector, create two fresh streams from a repeatable source, or materialize an intentional snapshot. I do not store a stream in a field for later reuse.

followups.q: Can a collection create another stream after one is consumed?
followups.a: Usually yes, by invoking stream again, subject to source state and mutation semantics.

followups.q: How can two aggregates be computed in one traversal?
followups.a: Use an appropriate collector, such as teeing, when its result and semantics fit.

questions.trap: Saving a consumed Stream and expecting to run another terminal operation later.
questions.notes: Unverified estimate; directly addresses supplied Streams GAP.

questions.question: How do intermediate, terminal and short-circuit operations differ in a Java stream?
questions.answer: Intermediate operations such as filter, map, flatMap, distinct, sorted, peek, limit and skip return a new stream and are lazy: nothing runs until a terminal operation is invoked. Terminal operations such as collect, forEach, reduce, count, min, max and toArray trigger the pipeline and consume the stream, so reusing it throws IllegalStateException. Short-circuit operations can finish without processing every element: limit and takeWhile are intermediate, while anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch, findFirst and findAny are terminal. Stateless operations such as filter and map handle one element at a time; stateful ones such as sorted and distinct need to see other elements and can hurt parallel performance.

followups.q: What happens if a pipeline has no terminal operation?
followups.a: Nothing executes; the intermediate stages only describe the work.

followups.q: Why is sorted a poor fit before limit on a large stream?
followups.a: sorted must consume every element before emitting any, so limit cannot cut the work short.

questions.trap: Calling short-circuiting a category of its own. It cuts across both intermediate and terminal operations.

questions.question: When do parallel streams hurt performance or correctness?
questions.answer: A parallel stream splits work across the shared ForkJoin common pool, which only pays off for large, CPU-bound, stateless work on a source that splits well, such as an ArrayList, an array or IntStream.range. It hurts when the data set is small, because splitting overhead exceeds the gain; when tasks block on I/O, because the common pool has few threads and is shared across the whole JVM, so one blocking task starves unrelated work; when lambdas mutate shared state or add to a non-thread-safe list; when encounter order matters; or when the source splits poorly, such as LinkedList or Stream.iterate. Inside a web request it also takes threads from other requests. For I/O, use an explicit executor with CompletableFuture.

followups.q: What is the alternative for parallel I/O?
followups.a: Submit tasks to your own bounded executor through CompletableFuture, or use virtual threads, so a slow call cannot occupy the common pool.

followups.q: Does forEachOrdered fix ordering?
followups.a: It preserves encounter order but gives up most of the parallel speed-up.

questions.trap: Answering that parallel is always faster on multi-core hardware. Splitting, merging and common-pool contention are real costs.

questions.question: How have Java's language and runtime features evolved from Java 8 to Java 21?
questions.answer: Java 8 introduced lambdas, streams, Optional and default methods. Java 9 added the module system, List.of and private interface methods. Java 10 and 11 brought var, the standard HttpClient and String helpers such as isBlank, strip and repeat, with Java 11 as an LTS release. Java 14 to 17 added switch expressions, text blocks, records, sealed classes, pattern matching for instanceof and more helpful NullPointerException messages, with Java 17 as an LTS release. Java 21, also an LTS release, finalised virtual threads, pattern matching for switch, record patterns and sequenced collections. Later releases keep previewing features, so state the release and whether a feature is final or preview.

followups.q: Which release made records a final feature?
followups.a: Java 16, with sealed classes finalised in Java 17.

followups.q: Why say 'final' or 'preview' when naming a feature?
followups.a: Preview features need flags and may change, so presenting them as generally available is an error.

questions.trap: Reciting features without release numbers, or presenting a preview feature as final.
